transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-22
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Zoe Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Halo Head of ML), James O'Neill (Halo Platform), Alicia Gomez (Halo Procurement), Ravi Sharma (Halo SRE)

Autogenerated summary (may be rough):
Halo is exploring Redwood as a replacement/alternative to their mixed setup (OpenAI + occasional on-prem). Primary focus is unit economics — per-token price, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, and whether Dedicated or Private gives them predictable TCO given 300M tokens/month baseline with seasonal spikes. Security (KMS, VPC) and procurement timelines discussed. Next steps: pricing scenarios, micro-benchmark, docs share.

Topics detected: cost per token, batching strategies, prefix/KV cache, dedicated capacity vs hosted fallback, private deployment constraints, SOC2/KMS, procurement windows

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm maya from redwood, i'm the AE on this account. quick intros?
[00:00:12] Priya Nair: hi, priya here, head of ml at halo. we've been evaluating inference options to get costs down while keeping latency for our chat/resolution flows.
[00:00:22] James O'Neill: james, platform eng — we care about SLOs, peaky traffic and locking down networking.
[00:00:27] Alicia Gomez: alicia from procurement, just here to listen on timelines / contracting.
[00:00:33] Carlos Ruiz: carlos, se at redwood. i'll be digging into the perf and capacity questions.
[00:00:38] Zoe Patel: zoe here, se, i'm on caching/quantization side.
[00:00:42] Ravi Sharma: ravi, sre. curious about fallbacks and monitoring.
[00:00:47] Maya Chen: great. goal for the call: understand your current cost profile and constraints, walk through hosting vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, and capture next steps.

[00:01:15] Priya Nair: quick context — we run two main flows: 'user chat' (~45 tokens input, 150 tokens output avg) and 'document summarization' (longer contexts), combined ~300M tokens/month today, with a 2x spike monthly on payroll cycles. latency SLO is p95 <= 500ms for chat. cost target is to reduce current spend by 30%. currently using openai for most but we have an in-house quantized runner for critical private PII jobs.

[00:02:10] Carlos Ruiz: okay that mix makes sense. for 300M tokens, batching and KV cache can materially drop per-token cost if you have repeat prefixes or across-session context. do you have percent of repeated prefixes vs one-offs?
[00:02:30] Priya Nair: roughly 20% of tokens are repeated patterns (prompts with similar system messages); the rest are mostly unique.

[00:02:40] Zoe Patel: that 20% is a good candidate for prefix caching — Redwood's runtime can keep KV cache across requests for a session or share common prefixes in a micro-cache. that cuts tokens billed for generation on repeats and reduces latency too.

[00:03:05] James O'Neill: when you say "cuts tokens billed" — how does billing actually work with caching? if the model reuses KV state are we billed on raw tokens sent or generated tokens?

[00:03:20] Maya Chen: good question — hosted billing is per-appearance tokens (input+output) but caching reduces the number of compute tokens because we don't re-run the prefix through the model; in practice you'll see both lower compute time (so lower cost) and fewer billable generated tokens in some internal models; we'll share the pricing appendix that models typical savings. dedicated and private usually give you a flat capacity cost + lower per-token compute if you bring quantized instances.

[00:04:05] Ravi Sharma: i'm worried about privacy — the payroll flows have PII; we may need VPC or on-prem. how invasive is the private deployment?

[00:04:17] Carlos Ruiz: private (VPC) means customer-managed networking, optional on-prem nodes for full data residency, integration with customer KMS for key management, and audit logs. setup time is longer but gives you full control. dedicated is a middle ground — reserved GPU pools under Redwood management but isolated by tenant.

[00:04:45] Priya Nair: operationally what's the difference in unit economics between hosted and dedicated for our volume?

[00:04:55] Maya Chen: high-level: hosted is pure usage, no commit, good for variable workloads but unit price is higher. dedicated requires a commit (monthly/annual) and gives lower per-token equivalent because you're amortizing reserved GPUs; we can run scenarios: for your 300M baseline with 2x spikes, dedicated becomes attractive if you hit sustained throughput and need predictable latency.

[00:05:30] Priya Nair: can you give ballpark numbers? even rough helps us converse with finance.

[00:05:36] Carlos Ruiz: sure — rough example (these are illustrative): hosted might be $0.0006 per token for a large-open model call; with batching/caching optimizations you might effective drop to $0.00045. dedicated amortized could push effective cost to $0.00025-$0.00035 per token depending on utilization and quantization. again, these depend on sequence length mix, batching headroom and whether you're okay with some quantization.

[00:06:08] James O'Neill: this aligns with our modeling assumptions — we had a spreadsheet showing ~0.0005 current. interesting that dedicated could drop to 0.0003 if utilization is high. what's the utilization threshold?

[00:06:22] Zoe Patel: typically you want 60-75% sustained utilization to hit those lower numbers. batching efficiency also scales with QPS shape — if you have consistent traffic windows batching helps more; if every request is single-user low-concurrency you see less batching uplift.

[00:06:45] Priya Nair: we have some predictable windows and some spiky ad-hoc support queries. are there autoscale options for dedicated? we don't want to buy too much.

[00:06:56] Maya Chen: yes — Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity. you can set a baseline and allow bursts to hosted pool as fallback. that's a common hybrid pattern for teams wanting lower committed cost plus protection against spikes.

[00:07:20] Ravi Sharma: what are the latencies like when failing over to hosted? we can't have 2s spikes.

[00:07:27] Carlos Ruiz: fallback routing prioritizes compatible model variants; there can be a small latency delta 100-300ms depending on region and model variant. you can configure circuit-breaker thresholds and warm fast-path instances to reduce that. we can instrument fallbacks and alert on them.

[00:07:48] Priya Nair: tell me more about quantization — you mentioned benefits but we worry about hallucinations/regression risk.

[00:07:56] Zoe Patel: quantization (int8/4-bit) significantly reduces memory and inference cost. Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles per workload and runs evals on your prompt sets to measure any regressions. for chat tasks we often see negligible quality delta with post-training quantization; for more sensitive NER/hallucinations we recommend running a controlled eval set.

[00:08:30] Priya Nair: ok that makes sense. we'd want Redwood to run a quick regression test on our prompts before we commit.

[00:08:38] Maya Chen: absolutely — micro-benchmark + quality check is standard. if you send the prompt set and a scoring rubric we can run hosted plus dedicated-backed quantized variant and give you P50/P95 latency, tokens per request, and quality deltas.

[00:08:58] James O'Neill: about batching — can Redwood batch across customers or only intra-tenant?

[00:09:06] Carlos Ruiz: no cross-tenant batching. Batching is intra-tenant and intra-model-variant. For private/on-prem deployments batching behavior is governed by your node configs. you can also set max-latency windows to trade latency for batch size.

[00:09:26] Priya Nair: curious about caching TTLs — we have frequent updates to system prompts for compliance. how quickly can cache invalidation happen?

[00:09:35] Zoe Patel: caches support granular TTLs and explicit invalidation APIs. updates to system prompts can invalidate a prefix cache immediately via API. there is a short propagation window for distributed caches but it's typically sub-2s for most configs.

[00:09:55] Ravi Sharma: security — KMS integration and audit logs. is the KMS only for model keys or also for data at rest?

[00:10:03] Carlos Ruiz: KMS integrates for encryption keys at rest and for transport-level keying where customers want to manage secrets. audit logs include token-level traces (anonymized on request), model versioning, and access logs; for private installs logs can be pushed to your SIEM.

[00:10:25] Priya Nair: procurement/paperwork wise — Alicia, any preliminary obstacles?

[00:10:31] Alicia Gomez: we need standard SOC2/ISO docs and SLAs; timeline depends on vendor terms. interested in a contract that allows staged commit — start hosted + pilot, then convert to dedicated with credit for pilot usage.

[00:10:45] Maya Chen: we can support staged agreements; finance often structures a pilot credit that converts if you move to dedicated. we'll loop in legal in the next phase.

[00:10:55] Priya Nair: what about monitoring and cost visibility? we need token-level spend per feature flag / domain.

[00:11:03] Zoe Patel: Redwood Console gives token-level cost breakdown, per-route/model dashboards, traces and alerts. you can tag requests with metadata (feature flags, tenant id) for attribution.

[00:11:20] James O'Neill: perfect. one more thing: for private/on-prem, what is the expected lead time and ops lift?

[00:11:29] Carlos Ruiz: private on-prem lead time is typically 6-8 weeks (inc. procurement, network certs, KMS integration). Dedicated can be done in 2-4 weeks with reserved capacity. hosted is immediate. ops lift for private is higher — you manage nodes, but Redwood provides orchestration tooling and support plans.

[00:11:52] Priya Nair: ok got it. can you run through a sample cost scenario live? numbers we can use for our spreadsheet?

[00:12:00] Maya Chen: yep, quick sketch: baseline 300M tokens/month, 45/150 token chat average. Scenario A - hosted only: $0.0006/token => $180k/month. With caching/batching 25% effective reduction => $135k. Scenario B - dedicated (reserved GPUs amortized): estimated equivalent $0.0003/token at 70% util => $90k/month, plus reserved capacity fee. Scenario C - private on-prem: large upfront engineering and infra, lower per-token compute but runbook + infra costs could push TCO close to dedicated for the first year.

[00:12:44] James O'Neill: that's helpful. i'd want to see those numbers with our exact seq lengths and spike profile.

[00:12:50] Priya Nair: plus we need to factor in risk: model regressions with quantization, fallback latency, and vendor lock-in.

[00:12:59] Zoe Patel: mitigate with canary rollouts, A/B evaluation on Redwood Console, and option to pin model version or force fallback to a different variant. we also recommend running continuous eval suites for production prompts.

[00:13:18] Priya Nair: ok, procurement question — if we sign a dedicated commit, how flexible is the contract if our usage drops?

[00:13:26] Maya Chen: contracts have tiered rollback/true-up clauses; we can structure a ramp and put guardrails so you're not locked into overcommit without options. we'll share typical contract language.

[00:13:38] Alicia Gomez: good. i will need sample SOW + pricing table.

[00:13:43] Maya Chen: noted. we'll send that.

[00:13:50] Ravi Sharma: one operational question — for the micro-benchmark, what telemetry should we capture?

[00:13:57] Carlos Ruiz: capture P50/P95 latency, tokens per request, CPU/GPU utilization, batch sizes observed, failure/fallback events, and quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/whatever your rubric is for summarization). also please include a 14-day trace to capture real spikes.

[00:14:20] Priya Nair: we'll prepare that and upload to the secure share.

[00:14:28] Maya Chen: great. any other questions?
[00:14:34] Priya Nair: maybe one — is it possible to do per-feature pricing (chargeback) so different product teams bear their own token spend?

[00:14:41] Zoe Patel: yes, Redwood Console supports tagging and chargeback reports per team/route — you can export and connect to your internal billing.

[00:14:52] James O'Neill: curious — competitors: how are you different from the managed endpoints from cloud providers?

[00:14:59] Maya Chen: we focus on inference economics and operational primitives: smarter batching/kv cache, model variant routing, and a single API across hosted, dedicated and private. cloud managed endpoints often lack the same unit-cost and batching optimizations or require more engineering to reach the same economics.

[00:15:21] Priya Nair: nice. one last quick ask: can you provide a decision matrix that walks tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated vs private for our profile?

[00:15:29] Maya Chen: we will. that's part of the pricing/scenario packet.

[00:15:35] --- wrap up and recap ---
[00:15:35] Maya Chen: recap — redwood: send pricing scenarios, SOC2/ISO docs, micro-benchmark plan; halo: send prompt set and traffic trace. agree to schedule a technical deep-dive next week focused on infra + onboarding steps.
[00:15:54] Priya Nair: yes, sounds good. thanks everyone.
[00:15:58] Alicia Gomez: thanks. we'll review and get back on timelines.
[00:16:02] Maya Chen: thanks all. bye.
